analysis.one_liner: Puts consumer-product-style safety rules, recalls, and fines on guns and ammunition.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 1998 by a single senator with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the Treasury Secretary — the agency that already licensed gun dealers — the same authority over firearms and ammunition that other federal agencies have over toasters, cribs, and cars: power to set safety standards for design and manufacture, order recalls or refunds of defective guns, inspect factories and records, and fine violators per unit. It also would have created a government clearinghouse for data on gun injuries, let private citizens sue violators for damages, and made knowing violations punishable by up to two years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun buyers and the general public. The bill's stated purpose was to protect the public from unreasonable risk of death and injury from firearms and related products, help consumers compare the safety of different guns, and restrict weapons that pose an unreasonable risk. It would have let anyone petition for a recall of a defective gun, sue violators for damages with attorney's fees available, and would have required the government to publish gun-injury data at least annually.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of the Treasury would have to issue regulations governing the design, manufacture, and performance of firearms, parts, ammunition, and BB guns as reasonably necessary to reduce or prevent unreasonable risk of injury.
The Secretary could order manufacturers and dealers to recall, repair, or replace dangerous or defective firearm products, or refund buyers' purchase price.
Any person could petition the agency to issue, amend, or repeal a safety rule or to require a recall, with a 120-day deadline for a response with reasons.
Violations would draw civil fines of $5,000 per firearm involved for the first five years and $10,000 after, and knowing violations after notice could bring fines and up to two years in prison.
Anyone injured by a violation could sue in federal court for damages, and any interested person could sue to enforce the act, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs.
The Treasury would maintain a Firearm Injury Information Clearinghouse, study gun-related deaths and injuries and their economic costs, and make the results public at least annually.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers. They would bear the cost of testing and certifying products, labeling, keeping records open to federal inspection, complying with safety standards, carrying out recalls and refunds, and paying per-unit fines — costs that typically get passed along in the price of the product. The bill also barred rushing manufacture or purchase of a product at an unusually high rate between the time a rule is issued and when it takes effect.

drawbacks.text: The bill gave one agency sweeping discretion: it could prohibit the manufacture, importation, sale, distribution, or export of any firearm product it determined posed an 'unreasonable risk' that other tools could not fix — a broad standard that critics of gun regulation worry could be used to restrict the availability of lawful guns, not just genuinely defective ones.

The compliance burden would be real: every manufacturer would have to test and certify each product, label it, notify the agency of new models, and keep records open to inspection, with a separate fine for each firearm involved — costs that would fall partly on buyers through higher prices.
The bill would have let private citizens sue to enforce the act, which raises the prospect of litigation pressure on manufacturers and dealers beyond what the agency itself pursues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: At the time, firearms were essentially the only consumer product sold in America with no federal agency empowered to set safety standards for the product itself or order recalls of defective units — so the bill's core idea, treating guns like every other consumer good, had real value for buyers. The costs are genuine too: an industry-wide testing, labeling, and record-keeping regime, and a ban authority written broadly enough that its use would depend heavily on how each administration defined 'unreasonable risk.' A careful version would need tighter limits on the ban power; this bill offered little.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Torricelli introduced the Firearms Safety and Consumer Protection Act of 1998 in the Senate on October 12, 1998, in the final months of the 105th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
No cosponsors signed on — the cosponsor list shows zero.
The action history records no further steps after the committee referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers and dealers came out ahead: the bill that would have subjected their products to federal safety standards, recalls, inspections, and per-unit fines never advanced, so the industry's products remained outside the reach of product-safety regulation. Ordinary consumers got nothing — no safety standards, no recall authority, no public gun-injury data collection.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 12, 1998 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association and the firearms industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed extending consumer-product safety regulation to firearms, viewing it as a vehicle for restricting gun sales; no such opposition appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected every gun, part, and round of ammunition to federal safety standards, mandatory testing and certification, factory and records inspections, recalls, refunds, and fines of $5,000 per unit — costs the industry has historically avoided because no agency regulates the safety of the product itself. The bill's death left that exemption intact.

Dealers and pawnbrokers would have faced labeling duties, recordkeeping open to federal inspection, liability for selling noncompliant products, and per-unit fines. The bill never advanced, so they faced no new obligations.

industries.industry: Nonpowder firearm (BB gun and pellet gun) makers
industries.note: The bill explicitly brought BB guns, pellet guns, and similar devices — a product category that injures many children — under the same safety and recall regime. It died, leaving them unregulated at the federal level.
